sections.title: The last first and the first last

blocks.text: Matthew 20 begins with a vineyard owner's repeated hiring of laborers and his decision to pay the last hired the same daily wage as the first. Jesus then predicts his death and resurrection, responds to a request for positions of honor, teaches servant-shaped greatness, and heals two blind men near Jericho. The chapter repeatedly redirects attention from rank and entitlement toward the kingdom's reversal of expected status and toward service.

sections.title: Labor and wages in an agrarian economy

blocks.text: The vineyard parable uses fields, laborers, wages, and the hiring of people standing idle in the marketplace. These images resonate with an unequal agrarian Roman-Palestinian economy shaped by labor, debt, taxes, estates, patrons, and dependent workers. The payment dispute is therefore framed through a recognizable contrast between those who bore the day's burden and those hired later.

Matthew 20:28 connects the Son of Man's service, giving of life, and ransom for many. That statement comes after the disciples' concern for status and Jesus' contrast between Gentile rulers and the community he is forming. In the chapter's own sequence, greatness is explained through ministry rather than through exercising rank over others.
